queries.text: How did American cities change across four decades (1980-2024): gentrification, inequality, affordability, and displacement — every claim cited?
Median household income by metro area for 1980, 2000, and 2024 from the U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey
Gini coefficient of income inequality at the metropolitan statistical area level for 1979-2023 from the Economic Policy Institute
Share of renter households spending more than 30% of their income on housing costs (cost-burdened) in major US cities for 1985, 2005, and 2023
Average annual percentage change in median home prices in top 20 US metros between 1980 and 2024 based on Case-Shiller or Zillow indices
Number of low-income residents displaced due to rising rents in specific neighborhoods over a five-year period using displacement index methodologies
Percentage point increase in college-educated population share in gentrifying census tracts from 1990 to 2020 compared to non-gentrified tracts
Median rent per square foot for apartments in New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago for the years 1985, 1995, 2010, and 2022
Ratio of median home price to median household income (affordability ratio) for major US cities calculated annually from 1984 through 2023
Count of households priced out of their previous neighborhoods due to eviction or sale between 2007 and 2021 in high-growth metros
Change in racial composition percentage points within specific gentrifying census blocks from decennial censuses spanning 1980 to 202

search_hits.title: Urban Gentrification Metrics: Four Decades of American City Transformation (the exemplar report)
search_hits.snippet: The operator's exemplar report (vendored as source-report.pdf): New York City leads with a Gini coefficient of 0.5469 versus the national average of 0.40 in 2013, while Atlanta and Miami follow at 0.57 and New Orleans at 0.56; the Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024 (+225% since January 2000); 48 of the 50 largest metros saw worsening mobility with Houston the sole improvement (+1.1%).

search_hits.title: Gentrification in America
search_hits.snippet: Governing analyzed Census tract data for the nation's 50 largest cities. Portland (58.1% of eligible tracts), Washington D.C. (51.9%), Minneapolis (50.6%), and Seattle (50%) led; nearly 20 percent of lower-income neighborhoods gentrified since 2000, compared to 9 percent in the 1990s; poverty rate percentage-point change -0.7 gentrifying vs +6.7 not gentrifying.

search_hits.title: City and metropolitan inequality on the rise, driven by declining incomes
search_hits.snippet: The 95/20 ratio for the United States was 9.3 in 2014 (up from 8.5 in 2007); among the 100 largest metro areas, 57 have a significantly higher 95/20 ratio in 2014 than in 2007; Atlanta and Washington D.C. are among the high-inequality cities.
